wu: Family Chain: Students stand in a circle. The first student says 'This is my mother.' The next student says 'This is his mother. This is my father.' and so on, adding one family member each time. They use possessive 's to link the previous person to their own family.
wuAlt: Find the Pair: Students receive half a family photo (e.g., 'My father') and must find the other half ('is a teacher') to make a complete sentence.
Speed Greetings: Students mingle and ask 'Have you got a brother/sister?' and respond with 'Yes, I have' or 'No, I haven't.'
pres: Show a large family tree flashcard. Point to each member and model sentences: 'This is my uncle. He's my mother's brother.' Drill the sentences chorally. Ask students to repeat and point to their own family members on the card. Check with thumbs up/down if they understand 'mother's brother'.
presAlt: Bring in a real photo of your family. Describe each person: 'This is my husband. He's a doctor. This is our daughter. She's five.' Students ask questions.
Use a simple story about a family. Draw stick figures on the board and label them with possessives as you read the story aloud.
prac: Possessive Relay: Divide the class into two teams. Give each team a set of family member cards (mother, father, sister, etc.). The first student runs to the board, writes a sentence like 'This is my mother', runs back, and tags the next student who writes a possessive sentence about another family member. The team with the most correct sentences wins.
pracAlt: Family Riddles: I write a riddle on the board: 'I am my father's mother. Who am I?' Students guess 'You are your grandmother.' In pairs, students write and solve riddles.
Find Someone Who...: Students walk around asking 'Have you got a [family member]?' and write names on a bingo grid.
ls: Listen to a short audio recording of a person describing their family. Students listen and tick the family members they hear (a worksheet with pictures of mother, father, sister, brother, grandmother, grandfather). Play the audio twice. Check answers as a class.
re: Family Charades: One student acts out a family member (e.g., cooking for 'mother', reading for 'grandfather'). The class guesses 'Is he your father?' or 'Is she your sister?' using target language.
prod: Thanksgiving Dinner Roleplay: In pairs, students are at a Thanksgiving dinner. One person is the host, the other is a guest. The guest asks 'Is this your aunt?' and the host responds. They practice polite dinner language: 'Can I have some more turkey, please?' 'Thank you for the meal.'
rw: Read a short text about a family. Students circle all the possessive 's (e.g., 'My father's name is...'). Then, they write 4 simple sentences about their own family using 'This is my...' and 'He/She has got...'
st: Read a short story about gratitude, like 'Thankful for My Family'. End with a one-minute gratitude share: each student says one thing they are thankful for about their family. Close with 'Today we learned to describe our family. Thank you for your hard work and have a great day!'
g: Students draw a 3x3 grid and write family member words. The teacher calls out clues like 'This person is your mother's mother.' Students mark the square.
A student thinks of a family member. The class asks yes/no questions: 'Is it a man?' 'Has he got a beard?' to guess who it is.
Wrap a box with layers of paper. In each layer is a family member card. When the music stops, the student opens a layer and makes a sentence with the card.
Students draw their family tree on a paper plate and label each member with a possessive 's sentence.
Each student adds one sentence to a story about a family, using 'and' or 'but' to connect ideas.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a short paragraph (5 sentences) about their ideal family dinner.
Support: Use a sentence frame worksheet with pictures to complete sentences like 'This is my ____.' and 'He/She has got ____ ____.'
hw: Draw your family and write 4 sentences: 'This is my... He/She has got... He/She is...'.
Write a thank-you email to a family member. Include: 'Thank you for... I love your...'.
Interview a family member in Arabic and write 3 sentences in English about them using 'He/She has got...'
tip: For adults, connect the family theme to their real lives by asking about their roles as parents, children, or siblings. This respects their life experience and makes the language relevant.
